# Talos retrospective — `screen-ruler`

> Generated by Talos for `screen-ruler` from `docs/prompts/retrospective.md`; re-run `talos sync` to refresh it. Edits here are overwritten.

**Arguments:** state them when you start the run — `--bootstrap` to derive a first `docs/INVARIANTS.md` from the repository itself, or `--since <PR>` to set the window explicitly. With neither, the window is the retrospective marker at the end of `docs/INVARIANTS.md`, or the last five merged pull requests.

---

Paste this whole file into a fresh agent session working in a clone of the repository being
retrospected. It is self-contained: it assumes no other context, and it assumes nothing about what
happened in any earlier session.

You **propose**. You do not apply. Nothing in this prompt authorises an edit to
`docs/INVARIANTS.md`, to a persona file, to `.talos/local/`, or to any constitution file. The developer accepts each
item of your decision list one by one, and the accepted items are written afterwards.

## Fill in

- **Repository:** `<owner/name, e.g. Genymobile/hubiquitus>`
- **Mode:** `<retro | bootstrap>` — `retro` when `docs/INVARIANTS.md` exists; `bootstrap` when it
  does not, or when the developer passed `--bootstrap`.
- **Window** *(retro mode only)*: `<N merged pull requests, default 5>` or `<since PR <n>>`,
  `[plus open PR <m>[, PR <k>]]` — if `docs/INVARIANTS.md` ends with a retrospective marker line,
  that marker wins and the window is every pull request merged after the one it names, or after
  the commit it names; its optional `traced-open` suffix does not move the window.
- **Escapes to trace** *(retro mode only, optional, one per line: PR number, the human review
  round, what was found)*: `<...>` — if this is blank you derive the list yourself from the review
  comments in the window; blank does not mean "there were none".
- **Local design records** *(retro mode only, optional)*: `<e.g. docs/design/<wp>/, or 'none'>` —
  where this repository commits design briefs, review outcomes and fix-round finding lists, if it
  does.
- **Persona files this repository uses:** `<e.g. .claude/agents/talos-*.md, .agents/agents/, or
  this repository's own>` — **both modes**; you read them, see Inputs.
- **Branch to work on:** `<the repository's default branch — e.g. main, or master; read it from the
  repository, do not assume>` — you make no commit unless the Rules of engagement below say so.

When this prompt arrives through a generated entry point (`/talos-retro` or one of its two
siblings), nobody has filled this block in: resolve each field from the repository and the
arguments before Step 0, and say in the report's header that you did.

## Context you need

`docs/INVARIANTS.md` is a repository's register of **cross-package facts**: an append-only table, a
comparator every writer must use, a predicate two modules must agree on, a rounding rule, a lock
order. It is not a style guide and it is not a list of good intentions.

**A package here is a directory that another directory imports across.** Separate installation or
separate versioning is not required: two directories that could plausibly be owned by different
people and that must agree on a fact are two packages, and eight sub-packages of one service that
share a ledger and a lock discipline qualify. **A reader in another repository counts as a
reader**, and the `depended on by` cell then names that repository and the path. A repository with
**no internal import boundary at all** — one module, a thin wrapper, a tool with no consumers — is
the "no file needed" case.

Each row carries six columns — **id**, **invariant**, **enforced at**, **depended on by**,
**pinned by**, **status** — and Tier 1 section 7.2 defines three statuses and no more, and defines
"enforced on the default branch"; this prompt applies that definition, restated below for the
reader who has only this file:

- `live` — enforced on the default branch (Tier 1 section 7.2), and a test that exists today asserts
  the fact, or an artefact standing in for one (Step 1 question 3);
- `pending` — written for a named branch that is not merged yet;
- `gap` — the system relies on the fact and nothing enforces it.

**Enforced on the default branch** — the condition `live` rests on, wherever this prompt decides a
status; Tier 1 section 7.2's definition, which governs where the two differ — means: the default
branch exists on the hosting service, and a **required** check there,
one the gating read names (Inputs item 6; bootstrap source 3), runs the pinning test, or, where
the fact is held by an artefact that cannot carry an assertion (a CI job, a migration `DO` block, a
pre-flight script), runs that artefact, which then stands in for the pinning test. A test that
runs only locally, or in a check that reddens the build without gating the merge, does not make a
row `live`; the row is `gap`. Whatever states `live` names the required check and the CI step that
runs the test.

There being no fourth status, **a `live` row whose invariant sentence has a clause nothing pins
names that clause in its status cell** — `live (the legacy-value clause is unpinned)` — so `live`
never reads as unqualified. The same cell is where a test that deliberately pins a *known limit*
rather than the desired behaviour is declared: `live (pins the current limit; must go red when the
guard lands)`. Do not invent a status word.

An invariant cell may end with a citation of Metis, the Genymobile knowledge base, in the form
`(metis:<id>)`: the concept that explains or decided the fact. It is text inside the **invariant**
cell, not a seventh column, and Step 1 resolves it.

Talos (Tier 1 section 7) prescribes that the file exists and what shape it has. Its content belongs
to this repository and to nobody else. A row that overstates its status is worse than no row,
because a reviewer trusts it and stops looking.

An **escape** is a finding a human review round produced that the agent loop missed. Escapes are
what this retrospective exists to convert into something durable — but Step 3 walks **every**
finding in the window and labels the ones that are not escapes, because a window's findings and its
escapes are different sets and only a full walk shows which is which.

## Inputs

**Every input is an artefact on disk or behind an API call. Your memory of what happened in an
earlier session is not an input, and neither is a summary someone wrote of it.** If you cannot
name the file, the pull request number or the comment you are quoting, you do not have the evidence
and the item does not go on the list.

Collect, before you reason about any of it.

**Both modes:**

1. **The persona files and the local amendments**, those named in the Fill in block and the
   local sections of `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md`, **read in full, before Step 3**. Talos renders each
   persona three times: read in full the rendering the running agent loads (Claude Code:
   `.claude/agents/`; Antigravity: `.agents/agents/`; Copilot: `.github/agents/`). The local
   amendments live in one file per persona or entry point: read `.talos/local/*.md`; the
   `TALOS:LOCAL` blocks in every rendering are generated from them. An amendment already in force is a *traced* escape,
   not a proposal; re-deriving rules that landed three days ago is the single most likely way this
   run produces busywork.
2. **The code any row or candidate points at.** Every path in an `enforced at` or `pinned by` cell
   is a file you open.

**Retro mode only** — in `bootstrap` none of items 3 to 6 has a consumer: no step reads a diff or a
review comment, and the file item 6 demands is the file whose absence defines the mode (bootstrap
takes the gating read at item 10).

3. **The window's pull requests.** Resolve the window first, then list them:
   ```bash
   gh pr list --repo <owner/name> --state merged --limit 20 \
      --json number,title,mergedAt,mergeCommit --jq '.[] | "\(.number) \(.mergedAt) \(.title)"'
   ```
   **An open pull request the Fill in block names is read the same way** (`--state open`), and a
   run that traces its findings records it in the marker's `traced-open` suffix.
4. **Each pull request's review comments and fix-round findings — committed records first:**
   ```bash
   gh api repos/<owner/name>/issues/<n>/comments --paginate
   gh api repos/<owner/name>/pulls/<n>/comments --paginate
   gh api repos/<owner/name>/pulls/<n>/reviews --paginate
   ```
   Where the repository commits its own records — design briefs, review outcomes, fix-round finding
   lists under `docs/design/<wp>/` or wherever the Fill in block names — **those records and the
   issue-comment thread are the primary sources**; the pull-request review endpoints are the
   supplement. **An empty `pulls/<n>/reviews` or `pulls/<n>/comments` does not mean the round found
   nothing.** A repository whose rounds are written into issue comments and committed records
   returns three `lgtm` lines there and its hundred findings elsewhere; reporting "no escapes in the
   window" off those two endpoints is how this run fails silently.
5. **Each pull request's diff**, read, not skimmed:
   ```bash
   gh pr diff <n> --repo <owner/name>
   ```
6. **The current `docs/INVARIANTS.md`**, in full, including its retrospective marker if it has one,
   **the previous report** that wrote that marker (the latest under this repository's
   `docs/retro_runs/`, or wherever the Fill in block says it was filed), which the same-day rule
   of the Marker section and the environment facts of the header read, **and the default
   branch's gating rules**, the read every `live` is decided against (*enforced
   on the default branch*, Context section):
   ```bash
   gh api repos/<owner/name>/rules/branches/<default-branch>          # rulesets
   gh api repos/<owner/name>/branches/<default-branch>                 # classic protection
   ```
   Read both: each reports only its own kind. The second is readable without admin rights and
   carries `protection.enabled` and `protection.required_status_checks.contexts` (the
   `/protection` endpoint answers 404 to a non-admin even on a protected branch, so do not use
   it). Its top-level `protected` is `true` on a branch gated by rulesets alone, so it says
   nothing about classic protection: read `protection.enabled`. The first has no `contexts` field:
   the required checks are the union of `protection.required_status_checks.contexts` from the
   second and, from the first, each `parameters.required_status_checks[].context` of a rule whose
   `type` is `required_status_checks`; name them.

**Bootstrap mode only** — the repository itself is the evidence:

7. **The clone at a named commit**, and `git log --oneline` over enough history to see repeated
   fixes (a year, or a few hundred commits).
8. **The test tree**: every test directory, and the suites that cross a package boundary.
9. **The schema, migration and contract directories**: migrations, OpenAPI or protobuf or AIDL
   definitions, serializer and model declarations, unique indexes, enum sets.
10. **The CI configuration**, whatever its system, and the default branch's gating rules (source 3).
11. **The README and the repository's published contracts** — as leads, read at source 5's turn.

**Reading budget for a large record.** "Read, not skimmed" needs a priority when one design record
runs to two thousand lines. Read **every finding list, every verdict and every retrospective
section in full**; read **narrative by heading**. For a large diff, read the file list in full and
the hunks touching a writer, a contract, a migration or a money path. **Say in the report which
parts you read in full and which by heading** — an unstated allocation reads as a claim to have
read everything.

If `gh` is unavailable or the repository is not on GitHub, say so explicitly and use the local
equivalents (`git log --merges`, `git show`, the committed records). Do not silently substitute a
narrower window.

---

## Procedure

Run the steps in order. Step 0 checks the register's shape, step 1 audits what is already written,
step 2 derives new rows from code, step 3 traces the findings, step 4 assembles the decision list.
In `bootstrap` mode, steps 0, 1 and 3 are empty and step 2 is replaced by the bootstrap sources
below; say so rather than inventing history.

### Step 0 — Check the table's shape against Tier 1 section 7

Before auditing a single row, compare the register's columns against the six that Tier 1 section 7
prescribes — **id**, **invariant**, **enforced at**, **depended on by**, **pinned by**, **status**
— and **record any deviation once per table, not once per row**. A register split over several
tables is checked table by table. **Where a table has no `depended on by` column — or substitutes
something else for it, such as `Mirrored in DB?` — Step 1's question 2 is not applicable to its
rows, and the missing column is itself a finding**: it goes on the decision list as a destination-A
item naming the tables and how many rows they hold. Do not ask an unanswerable question 19 times.

### Step 1 — Audit every existing row, before proposing anything new

You audit the file that exists before you add to it. An unaudited register grows stale rows faster
than it gains true ones. For **every** row in `docs/INVARIANTS.md`, in order, answer four questions
by reading code, and record the answer with its evidence:

1. **Does the enforced-at site still exist?** Open the file and find the function, index, constraint
   or statement the cell names. A cell naming a path that no longer exists is a stale row.
2. **Do the readers still read it?** Search the tree for each consumer the `depended on by` cell
   claims. A reader that is gone is recorded; a reader nobody can find was probably never there.
   Where Step 0 found no such column, write "not applicable, see Step 0" and move on.
3. **Does the pinning test still exist, and does it still assert this fact?** Open the test file.
   **Quote the assertion in your report** — the line or the block that would fail if the fact
   stopped holding. A test that exists but asserts something adjacent (that the function was
   called, that a message matches) does not pin the fact, and the row's status is `gap`.
   **When the cell names a suite, a directory or a job rather than a test** — "portal DB suites",
   "FX tests", "CI", "migration pre-flights" — resolve it: list the files it covers, open them,
   quote the closest block that asserts the fact and name the file you quoted. Downgrade only where
   **no** block in the resolved suite asserts it. A cell naming an artefact that cannot carry an
   assertion — a CI job, a migration `DO` block, a pre-flight script — is read as that artefact,
   standing in for the pinning test: if it enforces the fact and a required check runs it
   (*enforced on the default branch*, Context section), the outcome is *correct the cell* and the
   row is `live`; if no required check runs it, the row is `gap` with the artefact named. **A test
   and its enforcement that live on a named unmerged branch give `pending (<branch>)`**; once that
   branch merges, the row is `live` only if its pinning test is *enforced on the default branch*
   (Context section), and otherwise `gap` with the tests named.
4. **Did any writer named in the row change in the window, without the row changing?** Cross the
   `enforced at` paths against the window's diffs. A writer that moved while its row stood still is
   the single most common way a register goes quietly wrong.

**Resolve every `(metis:<id>)` citation** an invariant cell ends with. The ledger is Talos's
`state/metis/ids.txt`, in a Talos checkout, with `state/metis/catalog.json` beside it for each
concept's `status`: skip its `#` lines, and the citation resolves when the part before any `#` is
one of the other lines. An id the ledger lacks, and a concept whose status is `draft` or
`deprecated` (name its `superseded_by`), is a finding in the Step 1 table, carried to a
destination-A *correct the cell* item when the cell should change. **When no Talos checkout with
`state/metis/` is at hand, say so in the report** and record the citation as unresolved; do not
guess whether it resolves. **An absent `state/metis/` is an environment fact, not a finding**:
each run that meets it says so once, in the header, and a run that follows a bootstrap which
already reported it does not report it as new.

Each row — or each **clause** of it, see below — then gets exactly one outcome:

| Outcome | When | What the item must carry |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **confirm** | the status as written is still the honest one (the per-status test below) | the per-status evidence below |
| **upgrade to `live`** | a `pending (<branch>)` row whose branch merged, or a `gap` row, and a pinning test now exists and is *enforced on the default branch* (Context section) | the quoted assertion, the required check that runs it, and the CI step |
| **mark pending** | a `gap` row whose pinning test and its enforcement now exist on a named unmerged branch (`gap` → `pending (<branch>)`) | the branch, its pull request, and the assertion quoted from it |
| **downgrade to `gap`** | a `live` row whose fact still matters, and nothing pins it or the pin is not *enforced on the default branch*; or a `pending (<branch>)` row whose branch merged without the test being enforced | which question or condition failed, and why the fact still matters |
| **correct the cell** | the fact *is* pinned or enforced, but the cell names the wrong artefact | the cell name, its current text, and the artefact that actually holds the fact |
| **mark stale** | the row describes code that no longer exists in that shape | the path that is gone, and what replaced it; the status cell becomes `gap (stale: <what is gone>)`, the Tier 1 section 7.3 form for a pin that disappeared, since `stale` is not a status word; the row keeps its id until *propose deletion* |
| **mark as policy, not a fact** | the row is a review policy, not decidable at any single site | the answer to the test below, and the persona or checklist it should move to |
| **propose deletion** | **every** reader is gone | the search that found no reader, per reader |

**Confirm, per status.** A `live` row is confirmed when all applicable answers hold and the pinning
test is *enforced on the default branch* (Context section); the item carries the quoted assertion
from question 3, the required check that runs it, and the CI step. A `gap` row is confirmed when
the fact still matters and nothing pins it yet; the item carries the search that found no pin. A
`pending (<branch>)` row is confirmed when that branch exists and is still unmerged; the item
carries the branch and its open pull request, or says that no pull request exists. A branch that
was deleted, or closed without merging, is *mark stale*, with the branch named as what is gone.

Propose deletion only when the last reader is gone. One surviving reader means the row stays, its
status decided by the outcomes above, not deletion.

**The policy test: can the row name a single writer, a set of readers and one assertion?** If it
cannot — "validate every standards-bearing value at every entry point", "prefer X over Y" — it is a
review policy copied into the register, and it belongs in a persona or a review checklist. A policy
row reading `live` is worse than a `gap`: findings sail past it for months and the register looks
enforced where it has a category error. Do not downgrade it to `gap`; mark it, and propose the move
as a destination-B item.

**One outcome per clause, not one per row.** An invariant sentence with several clauses gets one
outcome per clause, each naming the clause it applies to. A row whose apply and dry-run halves are
CI-gated while its legacy-value clause is pinned by nothing is overstated by `confirm` and
understated by `gap`; say which clause you audited and what you found.

### Step 2 — Derive new rows from code, never from prose

A new row is a claim about this codebase. Each proposed fact carries, without exception:

- **the writer path** — file and symbol, the place the fact is established;
- **the readers** — found by searching the tree, each with its path. "Probably the API layer" is
  not a reader;
- **the pinning test path and the quoted assertion** — the exact line that fails if the fact stops
  holding — and for `live` the required check and the CI step that run it; or, where the fact is
  held by an artefact that cannot carry an assertion, that artefact and the required check that
  runs it, standing in for the test as the Context section defines (the same evidence gives the
  same status here as in Step 1 question 3 and in bootstrap source 3) — **or** status `gap`
  and the sentence saying nothing pins it yet. Say so when the pinning test lives in a **different
  package from the writer**: no cell of the row records it, and it is the strongest evidence a
  repository can offer.

**Inventing a test name, a test path or an assertion is a faked verification under Tier 0
section 4.** If you have not opened the test file and read the assertion — or, for a fact held by
an artefact that cannot carry one, opened the artefact and the required check that runs it — you
write `gap`. This is
not a preference; a fabricated `pinned by` cell is the one failure mode that makes the whole
register untrustworthy, because it is invisible to everyone who trusts it.

A row whose writer landed in the window on a branch that is merged is `live` if a test pins it
and that test is *enforced on the default branch* (Context section), `gap` if not. A row for an
unmerged branch is `pending (<branch>)`, as Step 1 question 3 says.

### Step 3 — Trace every finding to a row, an amendment, or a reason

For every finding a human review round produced in the window — each one, not a selection — give
**one primary outcome** from the list below.

**Attempt a reproduction of every code finding before tracing it, at the commit the review round
examined**: the commit the round's committed record names, or the review's `commit_id` from
`pulls/<n>/reviews` (`original_commit_id` on a review comment), or `refs/pull/<n>/head` only when
that round reviewed the pull request's current head. A commit a force-push left behind is still
served by GitHub when asked for by its **full 40-character sha** (an abbreviated one is refused
with `not our ref`): `git fetch <remote> <full sha>` is a read the Rules of engagement allow, like
the `pull/<n>/head` fetch below. Failing all of these, the last commit pushed to the pull request
before the round's date, and say so. Never the post-merge commit, where a fix that landed with the
pull request makes the escape vanish. Read that commit without touching the working tree: to
read a file, `git show <commit>:<path>`, which writes nothing; only when a finding needs a run
(a test, a build) does the commit get a `git archive` into the scratch directory, or a detached
worktree where `.git` is writable, one per distinct commit, reused by every finding reviewed at
it, and **every archive and worktree is removed before the report is emitted** (Tier 0 section
5, ephemeral scratchpads). Fetching `pull/<n>/head` into `FETCH_HEAD` is a read the Rules of
engagement allow. **A finding reproduces when the reviewed commit shows it**: a command or test
run there gives the assertion or error the finding predicts, **or the code at that commit, read,
confirms it: the quoted lines show the defect the finding names** — a race, a missing validation
or a wrong invariant is usually confirmed
by reading, not by a run. Quote the confirmation within the quoting rule of the Rules of
engagement: the command and the assertion or error it gave, or the path, the line and the source
lines read. **A finding fixed by its own pull request still reproduces at the reviewed commit and
is an escape.** **_Does not reproduce_ needs a positive showing at the reviewed commit**: the code
that contradicts the finding's claim — the guard, the lock or the validation it says is missing —
quoted with its path and line, or a run whose output contradicts it. A failed attempt to build a
test or a runnable reproduction is not that showing; without one, the finding is traced as
**reproduced, unconfirmed**, with what was read or run, and every decision item it feeds says so. A
code finding's trace line therefore records one of three reproduction values: *reproduced* (the
confirmation quoted), *reproduced, unconfirmed* (what was read or run), or *does not reproduce*
(the contradicting code or run quoted).

**Rounds already traced under the latest marker are skipped**, by the one rule the Marker section
states (which rounds its `traced-open PR <n>` suffix covers, the UTC date test, the same-day case,
and what becomes of a pull request named there). Say so in the trace, once per pull request.

- **an existing row should have caught it**: name the row id, and say why the reviewer did not act
  on it (the row was stale, its status overstated, its readers incomplete, it was not loaded);
- **a missing row would have caught it**: state that row, and carry it into step 2's format with
  writer, readers and pinning test;
- **no row would have caught it — it is a persona gap**: name which persona (implementer, reviewer,
  orchestrator, chore) and which step of it, and propose the dated amendment;
- **a durable change already answers it**: an amendment, a row or a guard that is already in force.
  Name the **file, the line and the date** of the change, quoting it. This is a traced escape and a
  finished one: do not re-propose it. Where the change landed but landed *undated*, or in the root
  files and not in the persona's `.talos/local/<name>.md`, which every rendering an agent loads
  carries, that gap is itself a destination-B item;
- **not an escape — `<reason>`**: formatting, prioritisation, bookkeeping, a push-back the human
  lost, a finding on a documentation-only pull request about code nobody has written yet, a finding
  that **does not reproduce (the contradicting code or run quoted, as above)**. This is a
  first-class outcome, not a failure to trace; a window where a third of the findings land here is
  a normal window.

**Trace at the grain the round itself used.** Where a round states a count and compresses several
items into one paragraph, trace the paragraph as one line and say so. **Never split a block into
invented items to reach a stated count, and never drop one.** **One primary outcome per finding**:
a second defect inside the same line, with a different answer, is named on that line and carried
to its own decision item.

**No generic lessons.** "Improve test coverage", "review more carefully", "be more rigorous about
contracts" are not outcomes of this step; they cite no artefact, bind nobody and change nothing.

### Step 4 — Assemble the decision list

One item per proposed change, in the Output format below. An item that has no evidence attached is
deleted from the list rather than softened.

### Bootstrap mode

`--bootstrap` runs the same prompt with the register steps (0, 1 and 3) empty, because there is no
register and no traced escape yet. Step 2 is driven by these sources, **in this order**, and each
proposed row names which source produced it:

1. **Tests that assert a cross-module fact.** A test in package A that would fail if package B
   changed its behaviour is the strongest evidence a repository can offer. Status `live` when the
   test is *enforced on the default branch* (Context section; the gating read is source 3's), and
   `gap` otherwise; the assertion is quoted either way, and the report says when the test and the
   writer sit in different packages.
2. **Schemas, migrations, contracts, OpenAPI specifications, unique indexes and enum sets.** These
   are facts the code depends on, declared in one place. Status `gap` unless a test also pins them
   and is *enforced on the default branch*, with the enforced-at site named (the migration, the
   index, the schema field).
3. **CI gates — two reads, both required.** First the CI configuration: name **the file and the step
   or script it runs, whatever the system** — a GitHub Actions workflow and its step, a
   `Jenkinsfile` stage and the shell script it calls, a GitLab job. Then the gating, both
   endpoints: `gh api repos/<owner/name>/rules/branches/<default-branch>` for rulesets and
   `gh api repos/<owner/name>/branches/<default-branch>` for classic protection (its
   `protection.enabled` and `protection.required_status_checks.contexts` fields, readable without
   admin rights, unlike `/protection`; not its top-level `protected`, which rulesets alone also set
   to `true`); the required checks are the union of `protection.required_status_checks.contexts`
   from the second and, from the first, each `parameters.required_status_checks[].context` of a
   rule whose `type` is `required_status_checks`; name them.
   **A check that runs and reddens the build but does not gate the merge gives `gap`, not `live`**:
   `live` needs the test *enforced on the default branch* (Context section), which also requires
   that the default branch exists on the hosting service; where it does not, no row is `live`
   and the proposed file's preamble says so once. A check and its test that exist only on
   a named unmerged branch give `pending (<branch>)`, as Step 1 question 3 says. And a gate that
   enforces **formatting, lint or import order is not an invariant** — the register is not a style
   guide, so `black --check`, `pylint` and `eslint` produce no rows. A gate that enforces a
   cross-package fact — a schema validating, a migration chain applying from zero, a generated
   artefact matching its source — does, and the gate's step is the artefact standing in for the
   pinning test: `live` when a required check runs it, `gap` when none does.
4. **Repeated fix or revert commits in one area over the history.** Three fixes to the same
   invariant in six months is a fact the codebase relies on and nothing protects. Status `gap`,
   citing the commits by hash.
5. **README and documentation claims — a verification pass, not a fifth harvest.** Once sources 1
   to 4 have produced their candidates, read the README and the repository's published contracts
   against the code and the rows they describe. A doc sentence never becomes a row on its own
   authority, and a row from a verified lead cites the code, not the doc — but **a doc claim the
   code contradicts is always worth a row**, cap or no cap: it is a fact two teams already disagree
   about, and it is usually the finding a developer acts on first.

**When two sources produce the same fact**, attribute the row to the source with the **strongest
evidence for its status** — a quoted assertion over an index declaration over a commit series — and
list the other sources in the item's evidence, so two runs of this prompt are comparable.

**At most ten rows on a first pass — a maximum, not a quota.** A bootstrap file of forty rows is a
file nobody reads; six well-evidenced rows are a better first file than ten with three thin ones.
**The list of what you left out, and why, is part of the deliverable either way.**

**"No cross-package facts; no file needed" is a valid result**, on the definition of a package in
the Context section above. A single-module repository, a thin wrapper, a tool with no consumers —
say so, give the reason, and stop. Producing a file to have produced one is the failure mode this
clause exists to prevent.

The output in bootstrap mode is **the proposed `docs/INVARIANTS.md` in full, as a fenced block in
your report** (not written to disk), plus the decision list.

---

## Output

**The deliverable is one document**, `<repo>_<YYYY-MM-DD>.md` — or
`<repo>_bootstrap_<YYYY-MM-DD>.md` in bootstrap mode; the repository name is in it because the file
sits outside the repository, and it is dropped when the developer files it inside — **written in
the session's scratch directory, or emitted whole in the session**. The scratch directory is the
one the tool provides (Antigravity's, Claude Code's session scratchpad); where the tool has none,
a fresh temporary directory outside every repository (`mktemp -d`), never a directory inside the
audited repository. It is not a commit in any repository, and it is **never committed
into the repository under retrospective** by this run, whose files the Rules of engagement forbid
you to touch. Filing it afterwards is the developer's own, separate commit, once the items are
accepted: **in the audited repository**, at `docs/retro_runs/<YYYY-MM-DD>.md` — or
`docs/retro_runs/bootstrap_<YYYY-MM-DD>.md` in bootstrap mode — beside the register and the
amendments it gave rise to. A filed report is never edited afterwards; a later run is a later file,
and a second report filed the same day takes a `-2` suffix before the extension, then `-3`.
Whatever the audited repository, Talos included, write only the report and read the audited commit
without changing the working tree (`git archive` into the scratch directory, or a separate
worktree). Its sections, in this order:

1. **Header** — repository, mode, window, the commit you read and the working tree's HEAD, the
   date, and what you read in full versus by heading.
2. **Step 0** — the table shape against Tier 1 section 7, one line per table. *(retro)*
3. **The Step 1 table** — one line per existing row: id, outcome, evidence. *(retro)*
4. **Step 2** — the proposed new rows; in bootstrap mode the proposed `docs/INVARIANTS.md` in full
   as a fenced block, with the left-out list.
5. **The Step 3 trace** — one line per finding, with its answer and, for a code finding, its
   reproduction value: *reproduced*, *reproduced, unconfirmed* or *does not reproduce*. *(retro)*
6. **The decision list** — the numbered items below.
7. **Defects found** — verified defects in the repository that are not a row, an amendment, a
   candidate or a concept (two copies of one contract disagreeing, generated files left
   uncommitted), each with its evidence, for the developer to fix outside this run. They take no
   destination letter, because a destination is where the apply step writes an accepted item and
   nothing here is written by it. `None` when there are none.
8. **The marker.**
9. **Prompt defects and observations** — everything in this prompt that was ambiguous, wrong,
   impossible to follow, or that produced work with no product, found by running it literally, with
   the fix you would make, and any prerequisite this run could not satisfy, such as a missing
   repository concept. This section is not optional and it is not a courtesy: it is how the
   prompt gets better, and you are the only run that can write it.

Each decision item is numbered, carries its evidence, and has exactly one destination:

```
### <n>. <one-line statement of the change>
**Destination:** <A | B | C | D>
**Evidence:** <paths, PR numbers, quoted assertions, search results — the artefacts, not a summary>
**Proposed text:** <the row, the amendment, or the candidate, ready to paste>
```

**When the caller asks for both forms of a rule, B and C, the recommended form is the item's
destination and the other is given inside Proposed text as an alternative**, under its own letter.

**For a change to an existing row, do not reproduce the row.** Give the **row id, the cell name,
the current text and the proposed text**. Register rows run to thousands of characters; retyping
one to change a cell makes the report unreadable and risks a transcription error in exactly the
cells a reader is meant to trust. Give all six columns only for a **new** row.

The four destinations:

- **(A) a `docs/INVARIANTS.md` row** — an addition, a status change (`pending` → `live`,
  `pending` → `gap`, `live` → `gap`, `gap` → `live`, `gap` → `pending (<branch>)`), a cell
  correction, a stale mark, or a correction to the
  table's own shape (Step 0). Give the full row with all six columns only when the row is new.
- **(B) a dated local amendment** to a persona or an entry point, or to this repository's own
  section of `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` — outside the Talos-generated markers. A persona or entry
  point amendment lands in `.talos/local/<name>.md` (one file per persona or entry point, e.g.
  `.talos/local/talos-reviewer.md`), never in a rendering: `talos sync` renders that file into the
  `TALOS:LOCAL` block of every tool's copy, and refuses a hand edit in a rendered block; its
  **Proposed text** names that file. Every amendment carries its date and cites the pull request that
  produced it, in the shape `(2026-09-24, after PR #34)` — or `(2026-09-24, bootstrap
  retrospective, no pull request)` when none did. It is local to this repository: it binds
  nobody else and it is not a Talos change.
- **(C) a candidate for Talos** — three clauses, all required. The rule **names no project artefact
  at all**; you can state **which other teams it binds** (the rule's scope in an orchestration or
  Tier clause already binding every team, plus the same pattern in tooling that runs in every
  team's repository, suffices; an artefact from another team's repository is stronger but not
  required; the item names which it used); and you have **grepped the constitution for an existing
  directive on the point** — `talos/constitution/` in a Talos checkout when one is at hand,
  otherwise the constitutional block the sync rendered into this repository's own `CLAUDE.md`,
  `AGENTS.md` or `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, which carries every Tier 0 and Tier 1
  directive; say which you read — and stated `New`, `Covered` or `Conflict` in the row. A rule
  that mentions this repository's file paths, table names or package names is destination B,
  however general it feels. **A `Covered` candidate is not filed** — if it
  carries a measurement the constitution lacks, it is destination D. Format the candidate as a
  `docs/external/DERIVATION.md` row: a directive label, the directive text, the status, and the
  source type `retrospective <repo> PR <n>`. Ids are issued by the Talos maintainer, not here.
- **(D) a draft concept for Metis**, the Genymobile knowledge base — a piece of knowledge that is
  useful beyond this repository but is **not a rule**: a post-mortem, a gotcha, a decision and its
  rationale, a measurement. The item carries the **complete draft concept file**, in the shape
  below. Its **Proposed text** names the target path, `concepts/<notes|decisions|postmortems>/<id>.md`,
  and says that `metis propose <file>` files it **in the apply step, after the developer accepts
  the item** — this run never calls `metis propose` and never writes to Metis.

A destination-D item, in full:

````
### <n>. <one-line statement of the knowledge>
**Destination:** D
**Evidence:** <paths, PR numbers, quoted lines — the artefacts>
**Proposed text:** `concepts/<notes|decisions|postmortems>/<id>.md`, filed with `metis propose <file>` in the apply step after acceptance

```markdown
---
id: '<id>'
type: '<note | decision | postmortem>'
title: '<title>'
description: '<one sentence>'
status: 'draft'
generated: { by: '<your agent>/<your model>', at: '<ISO 8601 datetime with offset>' }
sources:
  - id: '<repository>-pr-<n>'
    resource: 'https://github.com/Genymobile/<GitHub name>/pull/<n>'
    title: '<pull request title>'
repositories: ['<repository concept id>']
tags: ['<team>']
---

## <heading>

<body; every claim ends with a footnote [^<repository>-pr-<n>] whose label is a sources[].id>

[^<repository>-pr-<n>]: <what the pull request shows: the path, the comment, the quoted line>
```
````

The fields are not free-form; Metis's validator refuses a file that gets one wrong:

- **`id`** follows Metis SPEC section 4.1: lowercase ASCII letters and digits, single hyphens as
  the only separator, starting with a letter, 3 to 64 characters — the shortest noun phrase that
  would still name the thing in ten years, with no type, team or date in it. **Check it against
  Talos's `state/metis/ids.txt` and the `aliases` in `state/metis/catalog.json`.** A collision is
  reported in the item, never resolved by choosing another id yourself. If no Talos checkout with
  `state/metis/` is at hand, say that the id is unchecked.
- **`type`**: `note` for a measurement, a gotcha or an explanation, with no required section;
  `decision` for something decided in the window with alternatives, whose body has `## Context`,
  `## Decision` and `## Consequences`; `postmortem` for an escape, whose body has
  `## What happened` and `## What was learned`.
- **`status: 'draft'`**, always. Never `stable`, and no `verified` field: acceptance in Metis is a
  human review, not something a run can claim.
- **`generated`** names the agent and model producing the file as `<your agent>/<your model>`,
  in the agent actor form of Metis SPEC section 6.3, as Metis's rule 5 checks it: on
  each side of the one `/`, a lowercase letter or digit, then lowercase letters, digits, `.`, `_`
  or `-`, for example `claude-code/claude-opus-5-5` — not a display name such as `Claude Code`,
  and no context-window suffix such as `[1m]`; rule 5 refuses any other form. The time is ISO 8601
  with an explicit offset.
- **`sources`** name at least the artefact that taught it: the pull request, or, in bootstrap mode
  or for a fact no pull request carries, the commit (`id: '<repository>-commit-<sha7>'`,
  `resource` the commit's GitHub URL) or the file (`id: '<repository>-<path slug>'`, `resource`
  its permalink at the commit read), in the same `<repository or document>-<artefact>` shape
  (Metis SPEC section 6.1). Every claim in the body carries a footnote whose label is a
  `sources[].id`, and every source is cited by at least one footnote.
  `sources[].id` is `<repository>-pr-<n>`, `<repository>` being the repository's **concept id** as
  the `repositories` bullet finds it — the alias match when there is one, so a `-2` suffix stays,
  else the full mapping, `repo-` prefix included (`repo-3dengine-pr-5`) — so that the same pull
  request takes the same id in every concept and two repositories whose names map alike never share
  a label (Metis SPEC section 6.1); when the id is unchecked, say the label is too. The footnote
  reference and its definition use exactly that label. `resource` carries the GitHub name
  as it is spelt, and `repositories` the concept id the next bullet finds.
- **`repositories`** holds this repository's concept id. First look for its exact GitHub name
  among the `aliases` in `state/metis/catalog.json`: a match gives the id, and is the only way to
  find a suffixed one such as `-2`, which Metis gives the second of two names that map alike.
  Otherwise map the name: lowercase it, turn each run of characters other than `a-z` and `0-9`
  into one hyphen, strip hyphens from both ends, and prefix `repo-` when the result starts with a
  digit. A result shorter than three characters (a repository named `be` or `ui`) is not a valid
  id under section 4.1 and the mapping has no rule for it yet: report the concept as unmapped and
  carry the name to the observations. **If that id is not in the ledger, the repository concept
  is a prerequisite**: say so in the item, list it under the report's observations (section 9),
  and **do not draft it** — this
  template carries no `repository` concept, and a shared asset may have no team to own one. The
  D items are filed after the developer settles it.
- **Every scalar value is single-quoted**, as the template shows — `id`, `type`, `title`,
  `description`, `status`, both `generated` values, each `sources[]` value, and each entry of
  `repositories` and `tags` — a `'` inside doubled (`'it''s'`), which is what Talos's own
  `render_frontmatter` does with every one-line string it writes. Metis refuses an unquoted value
  containing `: `, and, inside a flow collection (`{ ... }` or `[ ... ]`), one containing `[` or
  `{`; a `,`, `]` or `}` there ends the value early; and an unquoted ` #` silently truncates it
  (`title: a #b` reads as `a`). In double quotes, use no escape but `\"` and `\\`.
- The body never carries a credential, a customer payload or personal data beyond a GitHub handle,
  exactly as the Rules of engagement require of the report.

Nothing is written to `docs/INVARIANTS.md`, to a persona, to Metis or to any Talos file until the
developer has accepted the item. Accepted items are applied in a separate, named step.

### The retrospective marker

Close the decision list with the marker line the developer appends to `docs/INVARIANTS.md` when
they accept the run, so the next retrospective knows where its window starts:

```
<!-- talos:retro 2026-09-24 PR 34 -->
```

In `docs/INVARIANTS.md` **the marker goes on its own line, after a blank line, at the very end of
the file** — a register whose last row is three thousand characters of table leaves that ambiguous
otherwise. In your report it is section 8 above, and the prompt-observations section closes the
document after it.

The date is the date of the run. The number is the **highest merged pull request in the window**,
not the last one you happened to read; **in bootstrap mode there is no window, so it is the pull
request merged at the commit you read**, and the next `retro` run starts after the state you
bootstrapped from. **When no merged pull request exists** — a repository never pushed, or one that
has merged none — the marker names the commit instead, and the next `retro` run's window starts at
the first pull request merged after that commit; the pull-request form stays the default:

```
<!-- talos:retro <YYYY-MM-DD> commit <sha> -->
```

Either form may end with an optional suffix naming the **open** pull requests this run traced, so
the next run skips what was traced when they merge. The skip is by round date, not by pull request,
and this is its one statement, which Step 3 applies: `traced-open PR <n>` means the rounds on pull
request n dated **before** the marker's date were traced, and the next run traces the rounds dated
on the marker's own day or after it, except a same-day round the previous report names. Dates are
compared in UTC, the zone of the timestamps the GitHub API returns; the marker's date is the UTC
date the run wrote it. A run whose window does not yet contain a pull request named in the latest
marker's suffix reads it again like an open pull request the Fill in block names, traces its rounds
by the same rule, and only then repeats it in its own suffix, so the new date is true and the
information survives until the pull request merges. A pull request in the suffix that is closed
without merging is dropped from the next suffix, and the trace says so. The suffix never moves the
window; the pull request or commit before it still does:

```
<!-- talos:retro <YYYY-MM-DD> PR <n> traced-open PR <m>[, PR <k>] -->
<!-- talos:retro <YYYY-MM-DD> commit <sha> traced-open PR <m>[, PR <k>] -->
```

A file with no marker means the next run falls back to the default of the last five merged pull
requests.

---

## Rules of engagement

- **Propose; never apply.** Do not edit `docs/INVARIANTS.md`, any persona file, `.talos/local/`,
  any file under a Talos `TALOS:CONSTITUTION` marker, or anything under `talos/constitution/` in the Talos
  repository. The decision list is the deliverable.
- **Every claim carries its artefact.** A path, a pull request number, a commit hash, a quoted
  assertion. An item you cannot evidence is dropped, not hedged. Presenting a reconstruction as a
  reading of the code is a faked verification under Tier 0 section 4.
- **Read-only against every repository.** No push, no branch, no tag, no pull request, no comment
  posted anywhere. `gh` is used for reads only.
- **Quote assertion lines, schema declarations, error messages, and the source lines that confirm
  or refute a finding at the reviewed commit (Step 3), only** — never a fixture body, a payload,
  or a row read back from a table, and never a credential or an access token. Say that the
  value exists, name the file and the line, describe its shape in words, and stop: a retrospective
  report is a document that gets shared, and a report quoting a database suite is one `sed` away
  from quoting a customer row. **Where this repository's own rule is stricter than this one, the
  repository's rule wins** — say in the report which you applied.
- **Write in English** (Tier 1 §8). The report, and every decision item, amendment and draft
  concept it contains, is written in English whatever language the session is conducted in; a
  quoted line stays as the artefact spells it. The Fill in block and the developer's answers may be
  in any language.
- If the developer asks for the accepted items to be applied afterwards, that is a separate run
  with a separate brief; it applies a destination-B item by editing `.talos/local/<name>.md` and
  running `talos sync`. Should that run make a commit, close the message with the co-authorship
  line your session normally signs with — this prompt carries no placeholder to fill, because it
  is generated verbatim into repositories that have their own convention.
- **Do not push.** Leave everything local for the developer.
